transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I guess what brings me in is I just haven’t had the push I used to have. I used to be the kind of person who’d get myself up and go to choir, or work on my quilting, or go visit folks when I said I would. Those things used to feel like part of me, you know?

But lately, most days I just sit at home with the TV on low. Not really watching it all the time, just having it there. And I know people are expecting me places sometimes, or probably wondering why I didn’t come by, but I just… don’t get myself moving. It’s not that I don’t know I should. I do know. I just don’t seem to have the get-up-and-go in me like before.
How long have you been feeling this way—weeks, months, or longer?

It’s been longer than weeks, for sure. I’d say it started building after I retired from the school office… that was a little over two years ago now. At first I thought, well, everybody slows down some when they stop working, you know, and your days don’t have that same shape to them. But it’s just kind of kept going, little by little, until now it feels like this has been my regular way for quite a while.
Have you or people close to you noticed any changes in your memory, concentration, or ability to follow conversations or tasks during this time?

I don’t really know how to answer that exactly. I mean, I wouldn’t say my memory is gone or anything like that. I still know what I’m doing, and if someone asks me something, I can usually follow along.

Sometimes I’ll misplace my glasses or walk into the kitchen and forget what I went in there for, but I kind of think everybody my age does that some. As far as conversations, I don’t think people have told me I’m not making sense or anything. I might lose interest or get tired of talking before I used to, but I don’t know if that’s concentration or just me not feeling much like doing things.

Tasks… well, I don’t start as many things as I used to, but if I sit down to do something simple, I can do it. So no, I guess I haven’t noticed a big change like that.
Aside from having less motivation, have you been feeling sad, down, or hopeless most days during this time?

I don’t know that I’d call it sad exactly. I mean, I have my moments, sure—everybody does, especially when you’re home by yourself and the day gets long. Sometimes I sit there and think, “Well, what am I even doing today?” and that can feel kind of heavy.

But hopeless? I don’t think so. Not most days. It’s more like… flat, maybe. Like I don’t have the steam to get up and do the things I know I ought to do. I’m not sitting there crying all day or thinking everything is terrible. It’s just that things don’t pull me the way they used to. So I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed being sad or down most days, not in that way.

When you do manage to do something you used to enjoy—like a bit of quilting or visiting a friend—do you still find it enjoyable once you're doing it, or does it just feel like going through the motions?

It’s kind of both, I guess, but mostly the hard part is getting myself to do it in the first place. Like with quilting, I used to have my things out and I’d be thinking about colors or what piece went where, and now I can sit there knowing the basket is right there and still not pick it up. If I do make myself start, sometimes it’s all right for a little while, but it doesn’t pull me along like it used to.

Same with choir or going to see folks. I know people are expecting me, and I’ll even think, “I ought to go, they’ll wonder where I am,” but then I just sit at home with the TV on low, not even really watching it much. It’s not that I hate those things now. I don’t. I just don’t have the push. The enjoyment is quieter, I suppose, and sometimes it feels more like I’m doing it because I should than because I really want to.
Have you or your family noticed any new difficulties handling things like paying bills, keeping track of your medications, or finding your way to familiar places?

Well… paying bills and medicine, I don’t think I’ve had some big disaster with that, not like getting lost somewhere or anything. I mostly stay around places I know, and I can get to church or the store if I’m going.

But I guess there have been other things people have noticed. I used to be the one who would help organize things, you know, with choir and little projects over at the senior center. I’d say, “Yes, I’ll call so-and-so,” or “I’ll bring this,” or “I’ll make sure the papers are ready,” and lately I just don’t keep up with it like I should. I mean, I intend to. I really do. Then the day goes by, or I put it off, and then somebody else has to ask me about it.

So I’ve kind of stepped back from leading choir, which feels strange because that used to be something people counted on me for. And the senior-center projects too—I don’t volunteer for as much now because I don’t want to promise something and then not follow through.

My church friends check on me more than they used to. They’ll call and say, “Are you coming?” or “Do you need help with that?” They’re kind about it, but I notice it. It makes me feel a little embarrassed, like I’m not carrying my part the way I used to.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep or appetite since this started—such as sleeping much more or less than usual, or a change in your appetite or weight?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed a big change with that, no. I mean, my sleep has always been a little… well, it depends on the night, you know? Some nights I’m up and down, and other nights I sleep fine enough, but I can’t say it’s suddenly much more or much less than it used to be.

And eating… I still eat. Maybe I don’t always feel like making a proper meal, but I haven’t noticed my appetite being gone or anything like that. My clothes seem about the same, so I don’t think there’s been some big weight change. If there has been, it hasn’t been enough for me to really pay attention to.
Around the time this started, did you receive any new medical diagnoses or have any health problems come up—like a stroke, thyroid trouble, Parkinson's, or anything neurological?

No, not that I know of. I mean, nobody told me I had a stroke or anything like that, and I haven’t had some new diagnosis that I can point to and say, “Well, that’s when all this began.” I still go to the doctor for the usual things people my age keep an eye on, but there wasn’t anything new that stood out to me.

I suppose if something showed up in blood work or one of those tests, they didn’t make a big issue of it with me. And I haven’t been told I have thyroid trouble or Parkinson’s or anything neurological like you said. At least… not that I remember being told. It’s more like things just started changing in my day-to-day, slowly enough that I didn’t think of it as a medical problem right away.
Have your family or friends mentioned that you sometimes repeat the same question or story without realizing you already said it, or that you forget conversations you had recently?

I’m not sure… nobody has really sat me down and said, “You keep telling the same story,” not like that. Sometimes people will say, “You told me that already,” but I think that happens to everybody now and then, doesn’t it? Especially if it’s something on my mind or I’m trying to make sure somebody knows the plan.

As far as forgetting whole conversations, I don’t know. I don’t think I’m losing conversations completely. I might forget a detail, or I might need someone to remind me what time they said something was, but I can’t say friends or family have been making a big issue about me repeating questions over and over. If they’ve noticed it, they haven’t said it to me in a serious way.

Over these past two years, would you say this loss of motivation and slipping on tasks has been slowly but steadily getting worse, or has it stayed about the same, with maybe some better and worse stretches?

I’d say it’s been more of a slow build, not something that happened all at once. It really started after I retired from the school office… that was a little over two years ago now. At first I thought, well, of course things feel different, because I didn’t have the same routine, the same place to be, the same people expecting things from me every morning.

But then over time I noticed I wasn’t keeping up with things the way I used to. Not like one day everything changed, more like little by little it got easier to put things off, and harder to get myself moving. There are some stretches that feel a bit better than others, sure, but looking back, I think it has been building since I retired.

It’s been going on since I retired from the school office… a little over two years ago now. That’s when I first started noticing things weren’t quite the same, though at the time I didn’t think of it as some big problem. I just figured, well, I’m retired now, my days are different.

But if I’m being honest, that’s the marker I keep coming back to. Since then it’s just sort of been building, little by little. Not like one sudden change, more like after I stopped working, things started slipping and it’s continued from there.

Have you or people close to you noticed any change in your ability to plan or organize things that involve several steps—like managing a project, following a recipe, or organizing an event—compared to how you used to do it?

Yes… I think that’s one of the things I notice more than I’d like to admit. I used to be the kind of person who could keep track of things at church, especially with choir—who was coming, what songs we were doing, what needed to be copied or set out, all those little pieces. And I helped with some things at the senior center too, you know, projects where you have to remember what you said you’d do and then actually follow through on the right day.

Lately I’ve had to step back from that. Not completely disappear, but I don’t lead things the way I used to, because I’ll say, “Yes, I can take care of that,” and then I don’t keep up with it like I promised. Or I’ll start, but then some part of it gets away from me. It’s embarrassing, because people were used to me being dependable.

My church friends, they check on me more now. They’ll call or ask, “Do you still have that?” or “Do you need help with this?” They’re kind about it, but I can tell it’s different than before. Before, they just trusted I had it handled. Now they sort of look in on me more, and I know it’s because I’m not organizing things the same way I used to.

{"intent": "Assess for additional cognitive domain impairment (language) beyond executive/motivation issues, which would support a dementia diagnosis over an isolated apathetic depressive syndrome", "question": "Have you or those close to you noticed any trouble finding the right words

Um… trouble finding words? I don’t know. I mean, I suppose everybody my age has that thing where you walk into a room and forget what you were going to say, or a name doesn’t come right away. But I haven’t really noticed it as a big change, not like people are finishing my sentences for me or saying I’m using the wrong words.

Sometimes I’ll pause because I’m tired or because I’m trying to get my thoughts in order, but I wouldn’t say the words themselves are gone. My church friends haven’t brought that up to me, at least not that I can remember. So… no, I don’t think that’s been one of the main problems.
Do you ever lose track of what day of the week or date it is, or find yourself confused about the time of day?

I don’t think so… not in any big way. I mean, I do sometimes have to look at the calendar, but I’ve always kept one around, you know, on the wall or by the phone, just to keep appointments and church things straight. So if you mean do I wake up thinking it’s Sunday when it’s really Wednesday, no, I don’t believe that’s been happening.

The date… well, the exact date I may not always have right on the tip of my tongue, but I don’t know that I ever did unless there was a bill due or an appointment written down. And time of day, no, I usually know if it’s morning or afternoon or evening by the light and my routine. I might lose track a little if I’m sitting too long or if the day is quiet, but I wouldn’t say I’m confused about it. More like I have to check, the way anyone might.

If someone reminds or prompts you about a task—like calling to say “don’t forget the choir music” or walking you through the first step—are you then able to follow through and complete it about as well as you used to, or do you still have trouble even with that kind of help?

Well… if they remind me, it does help some, I’ll say that. Like if one of the ladies from church calls and says, “Now don’t forget, we need the choir music,” then it sort of brings it back to the front of my mind. But it doesn’t always mean I carry it through the way I used to.

That’s the part that bothers me, because before I could be the one keeping everybody else straight. I’d know what needed to be done, and I’d have it ready, or I’d make sure someone else did. Now even if someone checks on me, I may still not keep up with what I said I would do, or I get partway and then need somebody to ask again or step in.

So I’ve stepped back from leading things with the choir, and from helping so much with the senior-center projects. I don’t like saying that, because those things meant a lot to me. But my church friends check on me more now than they used to, and I think it’s because they know I’m not following through like I did before.

When someone actually sits down with you and walks you through the steps of a task, like helping you organize the choir music step by step, are you able to complete it just as well as before, or do you still get lost or confused partway through even with that hands-on help?

If somebody really sits with me, right there at the table, it goes better than if they just remind me over the phone. I can do some of it, especially if they say, “Okay, now put these pages here,” or “This stack is for Sunday,” that kind of thing. But I don’t feel like I’m doing it just as well as before, no.

Before, I was the one who knew what went where, what needed copying, who needed which music, and I could keep it all in my head. Now even with someone helping, I may sort of lose where we are, or I’ll agree to finish the rest later and then it doesn’t get done unless somebody checks back on me. That’s why I’ve had to step back from leading things with the choir. Same with some of the senior-center projects—I just wasn’t keeping up with what I said I’d do.

It’s embarrassing, because those were things I cared about and people counted on me. My church friends are kind about it, but they do check on me more now than they used to, and I know that’s because I’m not following through the way I used to.

When someone sits with you and does most of the organizing, are you still making mistakes or getting confused about the actual steps themselves, or is it more that you just don't feel driven to keep going even though you understand what needs to be done?

I think it’s more the second thing, if I’m understanding you right. When somebody is sitting there doing most of the organizing, I can usually see what they mean—like, I understand, “This pile goes here,” or “These need to be put in the folder.” I may be slower, but it’s not always that the steps make no sense to me.

It’s more like… I just don’t have the push in me that I used to. That’s really what brings me in, I guess. I used to be up and going with the choir, or quilting things, or visiting folks, and now I know people are expecting me, I know I said I would help, but most days I just sit at home with the TV on low. Not even really watching it all the time. It’s just on.

And I’ll think, “I should get up and do that,” or “I ought to call so-and-so,” but then I just don’t. It’s hard to explain without making it sound like I don’t care, because I do care. I just don’t seem to have that drive to keep going like I had before.

When someone comes to visit you at home, or you're just sitting there with the TV on, without you having to plan or organize anything yourself, do you still feel some enjoyment or interest in that moment, or does everything feel flat and unrewarding even then?

I do feel some, I guess, if somebody comes over and sits with me. I don’t want to say there’s nothing there at all, because if one of the church ladies stops by, or someone talks about the choir, I can smile and listen, and part of me is glad they came. It’s just not like it used to be, where I’d get stirred up and want to jump in and help or go see somebody else afterward.

Most days, if I’m home, that TV is just on low. Sometimes I’m not even following what’s on it. It’s more like noise in the room. And I’ll know, plain as day, that people are expecting me for choir things, or that I used to quilt, or visit folks, and I’ll think about it… but I don’t get up and do it. That’s really what’s been bothering me. I don’t have the push I used to have.

So it’s not exactly that every single thing feels bad or empty. It’s more like the interest doesn’t carry me anywhere. I can enjoy someone being kind for a little while, but then when they leave, I just settle back into sitting there.

Have your family or friends mentioned any changes in your social manners or behavior—like saying things that seem more blunt or tactless than before, acting impulsively, or seeming less concerned about others' feelings than you used to be?

I don’t know that anyone has said that about me, not in those words. I mean, my family will say I’m quieter, or they’ll ask why I don’t come along to things, but I don’t think they’ve told me I’m being rude or saying ugly things to people.

I’m trying to think… because sometimes people can notice things and not come right out and say it. My sister might say, “You didn’t call her back,” or “You ought to thank so-and-so,” but that feels more like I didn’t follow through, not that I meant to hurt anybody or didn’t care how they felt. I don’t think I’ve been blurting out cruel things or acting wild or anything like that.

If anything, I probably say less than I used to. I don’t always know what to say, and sometimes I just sit there. But no, I haven’t heard that I’m more blunt or tactless. At least nobody has told me that straight out.
Have you or your family noticed any change in your ability to keep up with basic daily things like bathing, dressing, or personal grooming, or are you still managing those just fine on your own?

I’m not sure there’s been a big change there. I mean, I still do bathe and get dressed on my own. Nobody has to come in and wash me or lay out my clothes like I’m helpless, no. I can manage those things.

Now, I may not fuss with myself the way I used to, if that’s what you mean. Like, if I’m not going anywhere, I might stay in the same house dress longer than I should, or I don’t always fix my hair nice the way I would’ve for church or choir before. But I don’t know if my family would call that not taking care of myself exactly. They haven’t sat me down and said, “You’re not bathing,” or anything like that.

I guess I’d say the basics are still getting done, just maybe with less care or less regular attention than when I was out and around people more. If I have to go somewhere, I can get myself dressed. It just takes me a while sometimes, and I don’t put as much into it.

patient.answer:
Well… I guess what brings me in is I just haven’t had the push I used to have. I used to be the kind of person who’d get myself up and go to choir, or work on my quilting, or go visit folks when I said I would. Those things used to feel like part of me, you know?

But lately, most days I just sit at home with the TV on low. Not really watching it all the time, just having it there. And I know people are expecting me places sometimes, or probably wondering why I didn’t come by, but I just… don’t get myself moving. It’s not that I don’t know I should. I do know. I just don’t seem to have the get-up-and-go in me like before.

inference.note: Initial presentation of anhedonia/amotivation with decreased engagement in previously valued activities (choir, quilting, socializing); differential includes major depressive episode (single or recurrent), persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), mood disorder due to a general medical condition, or early neurocognitive decline given lack of detail on duration, medical history, and age.

At first I thought, well, everybody slows down some when they stop working, you know, and your days don’t have that same shape to them. But it’s just kind of kept going, little by little, until now it feels like this has been my regular way for quite a while.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know how to answer that exactly. I mean, I wouldn’t say my memory is gone or anything like that. I still know what I’m doing, and if someone asks me something, I can usually follow along.

Sometimes I’ll misplace my glasses or walk into the kitchen and forget what I went in there for, but I kind of think everybody my age does that some. As far as conversations, I don’t think people have told me I’m not making sense or anything. I might lose interest or get tired of talking before I used to, but I don’t know if that’s concentration or just me not feeling much like doing things.

Tasks… well, I don’t start as many things as I used to, but if I sit down to do something simple, I can do it. So no, I guess I haven’t noticed a big change like that.

inference.note: Patient denies significant memory or cognitive deficits, making dementia (F03) or mild neurocognitive disorder less likely, but cannot rule out yet given subjective minimization; chronic low motivation/anhedonia over 2+ years still fits persistent depressive disorder (F34.1) or depressive episode variants. I don’t know that I’d call it sad exactly. I mean, I have my moments, sure—everybody does, especially when you’re home by yourself and the day gets long. Sometimes I sit there and think, “Well, what am I even doing today?” and that can feel kind of heavy.

But hopeless? I don’t think so. Not most days. It’s more like… flat, maybe. Like I don’t have the steam to get up and do the things I know I ought to do. I’m not sitting there crying all day or thinking everything is terrible. It’s just that things don’t pull me the way they used to. So I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed being sad or down most days, not in that way.

Like with quilting, I used to have my things out and I’d be thinking about colors or what piece went where, and now I can sit there knowing the basket is right there and still not pick it up. If I do make myself start, sometimes it’s all right for a little while, but it doesn’t pull me along like it used to.

I know people are expecting me, and I’ll even think, “I ought to go, they’ll wonder where I am,” but then I just sit at home with the TV on low, not even really watching it much. patient.answer:
Well… paying bills and medicine, I don’t think I’ve had some big disaster with that, not like getting lost somewhere or anything. I mostly stay around places I know, and I can get to church or the store if I’m going.

But I guess there have been other things people have noticed. I used to be the one who would help organize things, you know, with choir and little projects over at the senior center. I’d say, “Yes, I’ll call so-and-so,” or “I’ll bring this,” or “I’ll make sure the papers are ready,” and lately I just don’t keep up with it like I should. I mean, I intend to. I really do. Then the day goes by, or I put it off, and then somebody else has to ask me about it.

So I’ve kind of stepped back from leading choir, which feels strange because that used to be something people counted on me for. And the senior-center projects too—I don’t volunteer for as much now because I don’t want to promise something and then not follow through.

My church friends check on me more than they used to. They’ll call and say, “Are you coming?” or “Do you need help with that?” They’re kind about it, but I notice it. It makes me feel a little embarrassed, like I’m not carrying my part the way I used to.

target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have for choir, quilting, or visiting folks, and most days I sit at home with the TV on low even though I know people are expecting me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the difficulty is due more to lack of drive or motivation despite understanding the task, which directly matches negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
I think it’s more the second thing, if I’m understanding you right. When somebody is sitting there doing most of the organizing, I can usually see what they mean—like, I understand, “This pile goes here,” or “These need to be put in the folder.” I may be slower, but it’s not always that the steps make no sense to me.

It’s more like… I just don’t have the push in me that I used to. That’s really what brings me in, I guess. I used to be up and going with the choir, or quilting things, or visiting folks, and now I know people are expecting me, I know I said I would help, but most days I just sit at home with the TV on low. Not even really watching it all the time. It’s just on.

And I’ll think, “I should get up and do that,” or “I ought to call so-and-so,” but then I just don’t. It’s hard to explain without making it sound like I don’t care, because I do care. I just don’t seem to have that drive to keep going like I had before.

doctor.intent: Differentiate global anhedonia (suggesting depression) from isolated motivational/initiation deficit (suggesting an apathy syndrome, e.g., early neurocognitive/vascular process) by checking if pleasurable experiences that require no initiative are still enjoyed
doctor.question: When someone comes to visit you at home, or you're just sitting there with the TV on, without you having to plan or organize anything yourself, do you still feel some enjoyment or interest in that moment, or does everything feel flat and unrewarding even then?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have for choir, quilting, or visiting folks, and most days I sit at home with the TV on low even though I know people are expecting me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether enjoyment or interest is diminished even when no planning or effort is required, which directly concerns negative symptoms such as reduced interest, pleasure, and motivation.

patient.answer:
I do feel some, I guess, if somebody comes over and sits with me. I don’t want to say there’s nothing there at all, because if one of the church ladies stops by, or someone talks about the choir, I can smile and listen, and part of me is glad they came. It’s just not like it used to be, where I’d get stirred up and want to jump in and help or go see somebody else afterward.

Most days, if I’m home, that TV is just on low. Sometimes I’m not even following what’s on it. It’s more like noise in the room. And I’ll know, plain as day, that people are expecting me for choir things, or that I used to quilt, or visit folks, and I’ll think about it… but I don’t get up and do it. That’s really what’s been bothering me. I don’t have the push I used to have.

So it’s not exactly that every single thing feels bad or empty. It’s more like the interest doesn’t carry me anywhere. I can enjoy someone being kind for a little while, but then when they leave, I just settle back into sitting there.

doctor.intent: Assess for disinhibition or loss of social appropriateness/empathy, which would support behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia over an apathetic depressive or purely amnestic dementia presentation
doctor.question: Have your family or friends mentioned any changes in your social manners or behavior—like saying things that seem more blunt or tactless than before, acting impulsively, or seeming less concerned about others' feelings than you used to be?

target_item.reason: The question is about changes in social manners, tactlessness, impulsivity, or reduced concern for others' feelings, which is not specifically covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that anyone has said that about me, not in those words. I mean, my family will say I’m quieter, or they’ll ask why I don’t come along to things, but I don’t think they’ve told me I’m being rude or saying ugly things to people.

I’m trying to think… because sometimes people can notice things and not come right out and say it. My sister might say, “You didn’t call her back,” or “You ought to thank so-and-so,” but that feels more like I didn’t follow through, not that I meant to hurt anybody or didn’t care how they felt. I don’t think I’ve been blurting out cruel things or acting wild or anything like that.

If anything, I probably say less than I used to. I don’t always know what to say, and sometimes I just sit there. But no, I haven’t heard that I’m more blunt or tactless. At least nobody has told me that straight out.

inference.note: Presentation is dominated by apathy/amotivation with mild executive dysfunction (planning, follow-through, organizing multi-step tasks) evolving gradually over 2 years, without prominent low mood/hopelessness, memory loss, language impairment, disorientation, or disinhibition. Retained enjoyment when passively engaged and partial benefit from prompting argue against major depressive disorder and against frontotemporal-type behavioral disinhibition. This favors an apathy syndrome (F06.8) possibly reflecting early mild neurocognitive/executive decline (G31.84 mild behavioral impairment/possible prodromal neurodegenerative process, F03.90 unspecified dementia given executive/IADL decline), with F32.8 (atypical depression with apathy predominant) and F06.1 (organic catatonic/apathetic state) kept as lower-probability alternatives given absence of clear mood or biological depressive symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine whether functional decline has progressed beyond complex tasks to basic self-care (bathing, dressing, grooming, hygiene), which would indicate more advanced dementia rather than mild cognitive impairment or an apathy/depressive syndrome
doctor.question: Have you or your family noticed any change in your ability to keep up with basic daily things like bathing, dressing, or personal grooming, or are you still managing those just fine on your own?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about basic self-care/activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, and grooming, which are not covered in the provided symptom profile manifestations.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure there’s been a big change there. I mean, I still do bathe and get dressed on my own. Nobody has to come in and wash me or lay out my clothes like I’m helpless, no. I can manage those things.

Now, I may not fuss with myself the way I used to, if that’s what you mean. Like, if I’m not going anywhere, I might stay in the same house dress longer than I should, or I don’t always fix my hair nice the way I would’ve for church or choir before. But I don’t know if my family would call that not taking care of myself exactly. They haven’t sat me down and said, “You’re not bathing,” or anything like that.

I guess I’d say the basics are still getting done, just maybe with less care or less regular attention than when I was out and around people more. If I have to go somewhere, I can get myself dressed. It just takes me a while sometimes, and I don’t put as much into it.
